title: Ethics as practice
hookLine: the second perfection: keep your precepts as a gift

lines: A RULE KEPT FOR YOUR OWN SAKE.
cards: A rule is usually something you keep for your own sake, or to stay out of trouble. Don't speed, and you won't get a ticket. Don't lie, and you won't get caught.
Now turn that around. What if every rule you kept were a present you handed to someone else?

Not to the police, not to a teacher, but to the stranger on the sidewalk, the person in the next apartment, the animal in the yard. That's the startling turn the Buddha gives to ethics. The perfections began with giving.
The second, ethics, turns out to be giving too, only quieter.

teach.b: First, the word. In Pali it's sila: ethics, good conduct, the way you live with others. It comes second in both lists of perfections, right after giving.
For lay Buddhists, it's shaped by the five precepts: not killing, not stealing, no sexual misconduct, no false speech, and no intoxicants that cloud the mind. Second, the surprise.
In a discourse in the Numerical Discourses, the Buddha calls these precepts five gifts. Keeping the first, not to kill, gives beings freedom from fear, freedom from hostility, freedom from harm.

The text says this gift reaches beings without limit, and the giver shares in the same freedom. Nobody near you has to wonder whether you'll hurt them. That's a gift, even if no one ever knows you gave it.

Third, the heart of the teaching. A verse of the Dhammapada, in Max Muller's old translation, sums it up: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened."

teach.h: STOP HARM, DO GOOD, CLEAR THE MIND.
teach.b: Notice the order: stop harming first, then do good, then the mind. Ethics is the ground the rest stands on.
Fourth, keeping them again. The precepts aren't vows taken once and forgotten. In temples and homes, they're recited again and taken up afresh.

A slip isn't the end; it's a reason to begin again tomorrow. After a week walking to Sarnath, Kushinagar and Vulture Peak, around an island and a mountain, the road turns out to be under your own feet.

how: Lay Buddhists take or renew the five precepts by reciting them in Pali or in their own language, at the temple or at home, and some keep additional precepts on observance days.

o: a code of conduct only monks are asked to keep
following rules to win the approval of a teacher
keeping the precepts as a gift of safety to others

games.q: ethics as practice: tap the pairs.
p: five gifts, in the Buddha's words

s: the precepts are only rules for keeping yourself out of trouble
the Buddha calls them five gifts: freedom from fear and harm given to others.
the Dhammapada verse begins with not doing harm
not to commit any sin, then to do good, then to purify one's mind.
once you break a precept, there is no taking it up again
Buddhists recite and renew the precepts, and a slip is a reason to begin again.

games.q: you keep the precept not to kill, and no one ever notices. by the Buddha's words, what have you done?
games.why: in the Numerical Discourses he calls it a gift: freedom from fear, hostility and harm, given to beings without limit, and shared by the giver.

practice: Let the breath settle, then choose one precept, not harming, not taking, honest speech, care with your body, or a clear mind, and say it quietly in your own words as something you intend for one day.
Bring to mind the people and creatures you'll pass today as the ones receiving it. They'll never know; it's still a gift.

wordCard.voice: Ethics as practice. Sila, the second perfection: keeping the precepts carefully, as a gift of safety and freedom from fear to everyone around you. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali sila (Sanskrit shila): ethics, good conduct, the second perfection.

carryVoice: Your line: the second perfection. Freedom from fear, handed quietly to strangers. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened.
